summary: This document describes a framework for supporting the Metro Ethernet Forum E-Tree service over an MPLS network. The goal is a simple approach to emulate E-Tree services in addition to E-LAN services on existing MPLS networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7387 describes how to build a one-to-many Ethernet service on an MPLS network. Each customer site is given one of two roles, a hub that may talk to every other site, or a spoke that may talk only to hubs. The document sets out the reference model and the two forwarding rules that enforce this, and explains what the current Layer 2 VPN work cannot yet do.

subtitle: How an MPLS network can offer a hub-and-spoke Ethernet service where the spokes cannot reach each other.

tldr.problem: Providers must offer a Metro Ethernet Forum E-Tree service, where each customer site is either a hub that can talk to everyone or a spoke that can only talk to hubs, and the Layer 2 VPN work in the IETF has no way to express that.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7387 extends the Layer 2 VPN framework with a reference model in which every attachment circuit carries a Root or Leaf role, and states the two forwarding rules that follow from those roles.
tldr.outcome: The document is a framework, not a protocol. It names the two gaps in the existing work, no role on an attachment circuit and no way to advertise that role between routers, and points to the requirements document for the missing pieces.

today: RFC 7387 is an Informational RFC published in October 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework document: it describes the model and the gaps in the existing work, and points to RFC 7152 for the requirements that a protocol solution would have to meet.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
The document describes a framework for the Metro Ethernet Forum E-Tree service over a Multiprotocol Label Switching network. The objective is a simple and effective approach to emulating E-Tree services alongside the ordinary Ethernet LAN service on a network that already exists. It extends the IETF Layer 2 VPN framework with a reference model and the functional components that go with it, and it points out the gaps in existing Layer 2 VPN solutions such as VPLS and Ethernet VPN that would have to be filled to support E-Tree.

The terminology follows RFC 4664, RFC 4761 and RFC 4762, with three additions. A Leaf attachment circuit is an attachment circuit with the Leaf role, meaning an Ethernet frame arriving at it can be delivered only to one or more Root attachment circuits in the same service instance, never to another Leaf. A Root attachment circuit is one with the Root role, meaning a frame arriving at it can be delivered to one or more of the other attachment circuits in the instance. An E-Tree is an Ethernet VPN service in which every attachment circuit has one of the two roles: a Root can talk to other Roots and to Leaves, and a Leaf can talk only to Roots.
sections.plainLanguage: The document explains how to give an MPLS network a new kind of Ethernet service, in which each customer site is marked either as a hub or as a spoke. The hub may talk to everybody; the spoke may talk only to hubs. The rest of the document is the model that makes this work and the list of what is still missing.

sections.title: E-LAN, E-Tree and the Existing Toolkits
sections.content:
An Ethernet bridge network is the one defined in IEEE 802.1Q: a frame is forwarded on its destination MAC address, reachability is learned in the data plane from the source MAC address and the port the frame arrived on, and a MAC aging mechanism removes inactive addresses from the forwarding table. Frames may be for a known unicast address, or unknown unicast, multicast or broadcast, and the last three are flooded to every port except the one the frame arrived on.

The Metro Ethernet Forum defines two multipoint Ethernet service types in MEF 6.1: E-LAN, a multipoint-to-multipoint service, and E-Tree, a rooted multipoint service. The Forum also defines roles for the User-Network Interface, the Ethernet interface between customer equipment and the provider edge, which is the same thing as the attachment circuit of the Layer 2 VPN framework. For an E-LAN service every attachment circuit has the Root role, so any of them can talk to any other, and that is what VPLS and Ethernet VPN deliver. An E-Tree service has one or more Root attachment circuits and at least two Leaf ones. It allows communication among the roots and between a root and a leaf, and it prohibits communication among the leaves.

The existing tools differ in how they reach that result. VPLS provides multipoint-to-multipoint Ethernet across IP and MPLS networks, forwarding on the destination MAC address and the VLAN, learning reachability in the data plane from the source address and the attachment circuit or pseudowire the frame arrived on, and aging inactive addresses out of the switching instance. Many providers have deployed it. Ethernet VPN adds active-active multihoming of customer equipment and uses the Multiprotocol Border Gateway Protocol control plane to advertise MAC reachability from an ingress provider edge to egress ones, so a router learns local addresses in the data plane and remote ones from the control plane; it was still under development in the Layer 2 VPN working group when the document was written. Virtual Private Multicast Service offers point-to-multipoint connectivity with several attachment circuit types, and for Ethernet it gives every multicast group in a VPN the same coverage, ignoring the destination address in the frame.
sections.plainLanguage: Two services sit side by side. An E-LAN is a flat service where every site can talk to every other, and the existing Layer 2 VPN work already provides it. An E-Tree is the same kind of service with a hub at the top: the hubs can talk to each other and to the spokes, but the spokes cannot talk to each other. Nothing in the existing work can enforce that yet.

sections.title: The E-Tree Reference Model
sections.content:
The reference model has three provider edges, each with a virtual service instance that corresponds to one E-Tree service. Customer equipment attaches to each provider edge over an attachment circuit, and every attachment circuit is configured with a Root or a Leaf role. In the example, six circuits are Root and six are Leaf. The rules that follow apply whether the sending and receiving circuits are on the same provider edge or on different ones.

An egress frame at a Root circuit must be the result of an ingress frame at a circuit with either role, attached to the same service instance. An egress frame at a Leaf circuit must be the result of an ingress frame at a circuit with the Root role. These rules apply to every frame type, known unicast, unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast, and for known unicast the forwarding within the instance is on the destination MAC address as usual.

Each virtual service instance keeps a MAC forwarding table that is separate from the other instances on the same provider edge, and it also records the role of its local circuits. A frame arriving from a circuit or across the MPLS core is forwarded to another circuit according to the table and the rules above, and when the target circuit is on another provider edge the instance sends it over the MPLS core. How that happens depends on the solution: one option is to mesh the instances with pseudowires as VPLS does and apply the E-Tree rules when forwarding, and another is to use the Ethernet VPN forwarding paradigm constrained by the E-Tree rules. Solutions that meet the E-Tree requirements would therefore be extensions to VPLS and to Ethernet VPN. In most uses an E-Tree has a few Root circuits, at the hub sites, and many Leaf circuits, and a provider edge may carry only Roots or only Leaves.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is simple: mark each customer connection as a hub or a spoke, and then apply two rules when forwarding a frame. A frame leaving a hub may have come from anywhere. A frame leaving a spoke must have come from a hub. The service instance keeps its own table of which MAC addresses are reachable where, so the two rules are enforced inside the normal Ethernet forwarding.

sections.title: Where E-Tree Is Used
sections.content:
The document lists eight uses. A hub and spoke VPN has the hub site as the Root and the spoke sites as Leaves. Wholesale access has the customer's interconnect as the Root and the customer's subscribers as Leaves. Mobile backhaul has the radio access network controller as the Root and the base stations as Leaves. Precision Time Protocol clock synchronisation has the time server as the Root and the clients as Leaves. An internet access reference has the broadband network gateway router as the Root and the subscribers as Leaves. Broadcast video, which is unidirectional only, has the video source as the Root and the subscribers as Leaves. Broadcast or multicast video with a control channel has the video source as the Root and the subscribers as Leaves. Device management has the management system as the Root and the managed devices as Leaves.

Common to all of them is that direct communication between Leaf sites has to be prohibited. For mobile backhaul the document notes an exception, since an LTE X2 interface allows communication between two base stations, and an E-Tree is appropriate for such a use. Also common is that a service may have one or several Root circuits, several being driven by a redundancy requirement or by having more than one serving site, and which applies depends on the application.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists the situations where a one-to-many service is the right shape: a company's hub with branch offices, a provider giving wholesale access to its own customers, mobile base stations talking to a controller, time servers feeding clocks, a broadband gateway feeding subscribers, a video source feeding viewers, and a management system talking to the devices it manages. In all of them the many end sites must not be able to talk to each other.

sections.title: The Gaps in Layer 2 VPN
sections.content:
Two problems stand in the way of emulating E-Tree with the existing work. The first is that the IP and MPLS Layer 2 VPN architecture has no distinct roles on attachment circuits and supports any-to-any connectivity between all of them, with no mechanism for forwarding constraints based on a role. The Metro Ethernet Forum service, by contrast, defines exactly two roles and derives its forwarding rules from the roles of the sending and receiving circuits.

The second is that no role is indicated or advertised. When a provider edge receives a frame from another provider edge over the MPLS core, it does not know whether the frame came from a Root circuit or a Leaf circuit, and the forwarding rules need that knowledge. The problem is sharpest when the receiving provider edge has both Root and Leaf circuits attached to the same service instance. It applies to every frame type, known unicast, unknown unicast, multicast and broadcast.

Some further requirements are specific to an IP and MPLS implementation. A Leaf-only provider edge is one that has only Leaf circuits in the service instance, and other provider edges need not forward frames that originated from a Leaf circuit to it, which may save network resources. It is also desirable for a solution to work with existing provider edges that support only a single role, where that role is the equivalent of the root. These requirements are set out in the E-Tree requirements document, RFC 7152.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are missing from the current Layer 2 VPN work. Attachment circuits have no role at all, so there is nowhere to record that a site is a spoke. And when a frame crosses the network, the router at the far end is not told whether the frame came from a hub or from a spoke, so it cannot apply the rule. The document also notes that a provider edge serving only spokes need not receive frames from other spokes at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An E-Tree service may be deployed for security reasons, to prohibit communication between sites, so a solution must enforce the E-Tree forwarding constraints. It must also guarantee that Ethernet frames do not leak outside the service instance to which they belong.

An E-Tree service prohibits communication among leaf sites but has no knowledge of the security constraints of higher layers, so in general higher-layer applications cannot rely on E-Tree for protection unless all the relevant constraints are implemented by the service itself.

Enhancing Layer 2 VPN for E-Tree inherits the security issues described in the Layer 2 VPN framework document, both in the control plane and in the data plane: issues entirely inside the provider network, issues entirely inside the customer network, and issues in the network between customer and provider. A solution must consider these and address them properly. VPLS and Ethernet VPN are the likely candidate solutions, and the security capabilities built into them are adopted along with them.
sections.plainLanguage: The service may exist precisely to keep sites apart, so the forwarding rules have to be enforced and frames must not leak into another service. But the service knows nothing about what the applications running over it need, so an application that relies on the service for protection must implement its own rules as well. Everything else follows the security rules of the Layer 2 VPN work it is built on.
